Thanks for reaching out about your customs bond. You can apply online here, and it only takes a few minutes:


Apply for your Customs Bond<https://www.keatingbonds.com/application-form?id=01t6A000004U1m5QAC&sc=US>

• Most importers need a continuous bond, which covers all of your entries for 12 months. The minimum is $50,000, or 10% of the duties, taxes, and fees you paid over the past year, whichever is higher.

• If you only have a single shipment, a single entry bond may be the better fit. Just let me know.

• Have your Importer of Record number (usually your EIN) and an estimate of your annual duties handy.

subject: Excavation Bonds and the Real Cost of a Utility Strike 🚧
body:
A look at shoring and lateral support bonds, new CGA damage data, and a little Thanksgiving cheer.


**Excavation Bonds
----------------------------------------------------

An excavation bond protects the public streets, utilities, and neighboring buildings adjacent to an excavation site. As a specialty bond, it extends surety protection to the municipalities and adjoining property owners who are not protected by the project's payment and performance bonds. Many municipalities and adjoining property owners now require one before work begins, naming themselves as the protected obligee.

Excavation bonds fall into two main types. 

 - Lateral support bonds, also called shoring bonds, guarantee that excavation will not impair the support of adjoining public or private property, and they are most often required on basement, foundation, and tieback work.
 - Street opening bonds guarantee that a public street or sidewalk is restored after utility or site work. Because cities title these forms inconsistently, the condition language on the bond form, rather than its name, identifies which obligation a permit requires.

The duty behind a lateral support bond is one of the oldest rules in property law. An owner may excavate for construction, provided reasonable notice is given to adjoining owners and the excavation is carried out in a way that keeps neighboring land and structures properly supported. Building codes reinforce that duty, and some jurisdictions set a stricter standard: New York City, for example, holds the excavating party strictly liable for damage to adjoining property, regardless of the depth of the work.

Underwriting reflects that engineering risk. Alongside financial statements, sureties look closely at the geotechnical report, the stamped shoring or underpinning design, the monitoring plan for adjoining structures, and a pre-construction condition survey, which records the neighboring property's condition before work starts and becomes central if a claim is filed. Support obligations also outlast the excavation itself, since settlement can appear months after backfill, so lateral support bonds are often held for a set period after final inspection.

Full Article < https://go.suretyplace.com/e/874891/excavation-bonds-/d4wyq/1672829217/h/AwqJ8HnQlf51JLU-3-M9-kj2hF6X79vBh_7e7BDL6DM > 


**What Utility Strike Costs Mean for Bonded Excavation Work
----------------------------------------------------

A new Common Ground Alliance report < https://go.suretyplace.com/e/874891/lion-annually-cga-report-finds/d4wyt/1672829217/h/AwqJ8HnQlf51JLU-3-M9-kj2hF6X79vBh_7e7BDL6DM > estimates that underground utility damage costs the U.S. economy $83.2 billion a year, nearly triple the long-cited $30 billion figure. From a surety perspective, the most telling detail is how little of that total is the repair itself. For every $1 spent repairing a damaged utility, CGA estimates nearly $16 more is lost to construction delays, business interruption, emergency response, and related disruption. Direct repairs make up less than 6% of the annual total.

Those downstream costs are where bonded contractors feel it most. Insurance may respond to the repair and third-party damage, but idle crews, schedule slippage, deductibles, and liquidated damages come out of working capital, the same capital that supports a bond program. Underwriters increasingly view documented damage prevention practices, such as consistent 811 requests, locate verification, and crew training, as a reflection of operational discipline. For excavation, utility, and site work clients, a well-documented prevention program and clean strike history can strengthen a submission and support future capacity growth.
